questionText: What is polymorphism in OOP?
option1: The ability for the same method call to behave differently depending on the object or arguments involved
option2: The ability to hide data using private fields
option3: The ability of a class to extend only one parent
option4: The ability to declare a class as final
correctOptionExplanation: Polymorphism means one interface/method name can take many forms depending on the actual object or argument types.

questionText: What are the two main types of polymorphism in Java?
option1: Static and dynamic typing
option2: Abstract and concrete polymorphism
option3: Compile-time (overloading) and runtime (overriding)
option4: Public and private polymorphism
correctOptionExplanation: Java supports compile-time polymorphism via method overloading and runtime polymorphism via method overriding.

questionText: Method overloading is an example of which type of polymorphism?
option1: Neither, it's unrelated to polymorphism
option2: Compile-time polymorphism
option3: Abstraction
option4: Runtime polymorphism
correctOptionExplanation: Overload resolution happens at compile time based on the method signature, making it compile-time (static) polymorphism.

questionText: Method overriding is an example of which type of polymorphism?
option1: Interface segregation
option2: Encapsulation
option3: Compile-time polymorphism
option4: Runtime polymorphism
correctOptionExplanation: Which overridden method executes is decided at runtime based on the actual object type, making it runtime (dynamic) polymorphism.

questionText: In the Student class with print() and print(String test), which is this an example of?
option1: Method overriding
option2: Method overloading
option3: Method hiding
option4: Constructor chaining
correctOptionExplanation: Two methods with the same name but different parameter lists in the same class is method overloading.

questionText: Given `Dog d1 = new Labrador(); d1.doBark();` where Labrador overrides doBark(), whose version runs?
option1: Dog's version, since the reference type is Dog
option2: Both versions run
option3: A compile-time error occurs
option4: Labrador's overridden version
correctOptionExplanation: Runtime polymorphism means the JVM calls the method based on the actual object's type (Labrador), not the reference type (Dog).

questionText: What is this behavior of calling the overridden method based on actual object type called?
option1: Field hiding
option2: Static method dispatch
option3: Constructor chaining
option4: Dynamic method dispatch
correctOptionExplanation: Dynamic method dispatch is the mechanism by which the JVM resolves overridden methods at runtime based on the object's actual class.

questionText: In DogSoundManager.makeSound(IDog dog), why does the parameter type IDog matter?
option1: It restricts makeSound to only accept the IDog class itself
option2: It prevents any subclass from being passed in
option3: It forces makeSound to be static
option4: It lets makeSound accept any class implementing IDog (Labrador, Pomeranian, etc.), enabling polymorphic behavior
correctOptionExplanation: Accepting the interface type IDog lets the method work polymorphically with any current or future implementing class, without needing an overload per dog type.

questionText: Why doesn't DogSoundManager need a separate makeSound() overload for Labrador and Pomeranian?
option1: Because both implement IDog, so a single method accepting IDog covers all current and future dog types polymorphically
option2: Because Java automatically generates overloads for subclasses
option3: Because makeSound is a static method
option4: Because Labrador and Pomeranian are identical classes
correctOptionExplanation: This is the core benefit of polymorphism: one method written against the interface works for any implementing class without code duplication.

questionText: What determines which overloaded method is selected at compile time?
option1: The name of the local variable
option2: The return type of the method only
option3: The number and types of arguments passed at the call site
option4: The order methods are declared in the file
correctOptionExplanation: Overload resolution is based on matching the argument list (count and types) to the most specific matching method signature.

questionText: Can two overloaded methods differ only by their return type (same name, same parameters)?
option1: Yes, but only if one is abstract
option2: Yes, but only for static methods
option3: Yes, that's a valid overload
option4: No, this causes a compile-time error since return type alone isn't part of the method signature
correctOptionExplanation: Java's method signature consists of the method name and parameter types; return type alone cannot distinguish overloads, causing ambiguity/compile error.

questionText: What binding is used for overloaded methods?
option1: Reflection-based binding
option2: No binding is required
option3: Dynamic (late) binding, resolved at runtime
option4: Static (early) binding, resolved at compile time
correctOptionExplanation: Overloaded methods are resolved at compile time using static binding, since the compiler picks the exact method based on argument types.

questionText: What binding is used for overridden methods?
option1: Static (early) binding, resolved at compile time
option2: Dynamic (late) binding, resolved at runtime via the actual object type
option3: Binding never happens for overridden methods
option4: Binding depends on the access modifier only
correctOptionExplanation: Overridden methods use dynamic/late binding: the JVM decides which implementation to call at runtime based on the real object.

questionText: Can constructors be overloaded in Java?
option1: Yes, but only in abstract classes
option2: No, only methods can be overloaded
option3: Yes, a class can have multiple constructors with different parameter lists
option4: No, constructors can only be overridden
correctOptionExplanation: Constructor overloading is common and valid, e.g., Student(String name) and Student(String name, int age).

questionText: Why might you declare a variable as an interface type (e.g., IDog d) instead of the concrete class (Labrador)?
option1: To enable polymorphic substitution, letting the same variable later hold any IDog implementation without changing the code
option2: Because interfaces run faster at runtime
option3: Because concrete classes cannot be used as variable types
option4: Because it avoids the need for a constructor
correctOptionExplanation: Coding to the interface/abstraction lets you swap in different implementations (Labrador, Pomeranian) without touching the code that uses the variable.

questionText: Does Java support user-defined operator overloading (like C++'s operator+)?
option1: Yes, but only inside interfaces
option2: No, Java does not allow programmers to overload operators themselves
option3: Yes, fully supported for all operators
option4: Yes, but only for the + operator on custom classes
correctOptionExplanation: Unlike C++, Java doesn't let developers overload operators; the only built-in exception is + being overloaded internally for String concatenation.

questionText: What happens to overload resolution when you pass `null` and there are multiple applicable reference-type overloads?
option1: It silently picks the String overload
option2: It always throws a NullPointerException at runtime
option3: Java always picks the first declared overload
option4: It can cause ambiguity and a compile-time error since the compiler can't determine which overload is most specific
correctOptionExplanation: Passing null with multiple equally applicable reference-type overloads is ambiguous to the compiler and fails to compile unless one overload is unambiguously more specific.

questionText: Can an overriding method change its return type from the superclass method?
option1: Only to a covariant (subtype) return type, not to an unrelated type
option2: No, overriding never allows any change
option3: Yes, but only to void
option4: Yes, to any return type freely
correctOptionExplanation: Since Java 5, overriding methods may return a subtype of the original return type (covariant return type), but not an unrelated type.

questionText: Can two overloaded methods in the same class return different, unrelated types?
option1: Only if marked with @Override
option2: No, all overloads must share the same return type
option3: Yes, overloaded methods can freely differ in return type as long as parameters differ
option4: No, only interfaces allow this
correctOptionExplanation: Overloading only requires different parameter lists; return types can vary freely between overloads.

questionText: What key benefit does polymorphism provide for extending a codebase?
option1: It prevents any further subclassing
option2: It removes the need to write any new classes ever
option3: New classes implementing an existing interface can be added without modifying the code that already uses that interface
option4: It automatically makes all methods static
correctOptionExplanation: Because callers depend only on the interface/contract, new implementations (like a new dog breed or discount type) can be added without touching existing calling code — aligned with the Open/Closed Principle.

questionText: Is it possible to achieve polymorphism without any inheritance or interface relationship?
option1: No, polymorphism in Java requires an IS-A relationship via inheritance or interface implementation
option2: Yes, using only static methods
option3: Yes, using only private fields
option4: Yes, any two unrelated classes are automatically polymorphic
correctOptionExplanation: Subtype (runtime) polymorphism specifically depends on a class hierarchy or interface implementation establishing an IS-A relationship.

questionText: Why is heavy use of instanceof checks with type-casting often considered an anti-pattern with polymorphism?
option1: It defeats the purpose of polymorphism by hardcoding type-specific behavior instead of letting overridden methods handle it
option2: It is required for all polymorphic code
option3: instanceof is illegal in Java
option4: It always causes a runtime crash
correctOptionExplanation: Relying on instanceof and manual casting to branch behavior duplicates what overriding is meant to handle automatically, making code harder to extend.

questionText: Do static methods participate in runtime polymorphism (overriding)?
option1: Yes, exactly like instance methods
option2: Only in abstract classes
option3: Only if marked @Override
option4: No, static methods are resolved at compile time based on reference type (method hiding, not overriding)
correctOptionExplanation: Static methods can't be overridden; a same-signature static method in a subclass merely hides the parent's version, resolved statically.

questionText: Are instance fields resolved polymorphically like overridden methods?
option1: Only public fields are polymorphic
option2: Yes, fields are fully polymorphic
option3: Only final fields are polymorphic
option4: No, field access is resolved at compile time based on the reference type, not the runtime object
correctOptionExplanation: Unlike methods, fields don't participate in dynamic dispatch; accessing a field always uses the declared (reference) type, not the actual object type.

questionText: What is 'parametric polymorphism' in Java typically implemented through?
option1: Method overloading only
option2: Generics (e.g., List<T>)
option3: Constructors only
option4: Static blocks
correctOptionExplanation: Generics let a single class or method work across many types safely — this is parametric polymorphism.

questionText: What does `<T extends Comparable<T>>` represent in a generic method?
option1: A bounded type parameter restricting T to types that implement Comparable
option2: An overloaded constructor
option3: An abstract method declaration
option4: A static import
correctOptionExplanation: Bounded type parameters restrict generics to a family of types, here requiring T to be Comparable to itself.

questionText: What does the wildcard `? extends Number` mean in generics?
option1: An unknown type that must be exactly Number
option2: A type that extends every class
option3: An unknown type that is Number or a subtype of Number (upper-bounded wildcard)
option4: A syntax error
correctOptionExplanation: `? extends Number` is an upper-bounded wildcard, accepting Number or any of its subtypes, commonly used for read-only generic collections.

questionText: What is a 'covariant return type' example when overriding?
option1: A method that returns two values simultaneously
option2: A method that returns a completely unrelated class
option3: A method in Animal returns Animal, but the override in Dog returns Dog (a subtype)
option4: A method that must always return void
correctOptionExplanation: Covariant return types let an overriding method narrow the return type to a subtype of the original declared return type.

questionText: Which of these best illustrates polymorphism through interfaces in a discount system?
option1: IDiscount ds = new MembershipDiscount(); and later swapping in CreditCardDiscount without changing calling code
option2: Making getDiscount() a static method
option3: Using instanceof to check the discount type before calling getDiscount()
option4: Declaring ds as MembershipDiscount and never changing it
correctOptionExplanation: Programming against the IDiscount interface lets the same calling code work with any implementation swapped in, which is the essence of polymorphism.

questionText: What is the term for calling the correct overridden method based on the object's real type at runtime?
option1: Late binding (dynamic binding)
option2: Early binding (static binding)
option3: Constructor chaining
option4: Field hiding
correctOptionExplanation: Late/dynamic binding defers method resolution to runtime, based on the actual object, which is how overriding works.

questionText: What is the term for resolving overloaded methods at compile time?
option1: Early binding (static binding)
option2: Late binding (dynamic binding)
option3: Reflection binding
option4: Lazy binding
correctOptionExplanation: Early/static binding resolves the exact method to call during compilation, which is how overload resolution works.

questionText: Which principle from software design does polymorphism most directly support?
option1: Open/Closed Principle — open for extension, closed for modification
option2: Single Responsibility Principle only
option3: YAGNI
option4: DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) exclusively
correctOptionExplanation: Polymorphism allows adding new behavior (new subclasses) without modifying existing code that depends on the shared interface, directly supporting the Open/Closed Principle.

questionText: If Labrador and Pomeranian both implement IDog, can a List<IDog> hold both types together?
option1: Yes, since both are valid IDog implementations, they can be stored and iterated polymorphically in the same list
option2: Only if they extend the same abstract class as well
option3: No, a list can only hold one concrete type at a time
option4: No, interfaces cannot be used as generic type parameters
correctOptionExplanation: A collection typed to an interface can hold any mixture of objects implementing that interface, iterating and calling shared methods polymorphically.

questionText: What happens if a subclass method has the same name as a superclass method but a different parameter list?
option1: It silently deletes the superclass method
option2: It causes a compile-time error
option3: It's overloading in the subclass, not overriding, since the signatures differ
option4: It's automatically treated as overriding
correctOptionExplanation: Same name but different parameters means the subclass method overloads rather than overrides the superclass method.

questionText: Why is 'program to an interface, not an implementation' closely tied to polymorphism?
option1: It means you should never use interfaces
option2: It only applies to static methods
option3: Coding against interfaces lets the actual implementation vary and be swapped at runtime without changing dependent code
option4: It means abstract classes are forbidden
correctOptionExplanation: This principle is essentially describing polymorphism: depending on the abstraction (interface) rather than a specific class enables flexible, swappable behavior.

questionText: In `s1.print()` vs `s1.print("Math")` on a Student object, how is the correct method chosen?
option1: Randomly by the JVM
option2: By the order methods appear in the file
option3: At compile time, based on the number/type of arguments in the call
option4: At runtime, based on the object's actual class
correctOptionExplanation: Since this is overloading (not overriding), the compiler picks the matching print() method based on the arguments supplied at the call site.

questionText: Can an abstract method be involved in runtime polymorphism?
option1: Yes, an abstract method's concrete override in a subclass is invoked polymorphically through the supertype reference
option2: No, abstract methods can never be involved in polymorphism
option3: Only in interfaces, never in abstract classes
option4: Only if the abstract method is static
correctOptionExplanation: Abstract methods exist precisely to be overridden by subclasses, and calls through a supertype reference dispatch to the actual subclass's implementation at runtime.

questionText: What is 'ad-hoc polymorphism' another name for?
option1: Generic programming
option2: Method overriding
option3: Interface inheritance
option4: Method overloading
correctOptionExplanation: Ad-hoc polymorphism refers to a function/method behaving differently based on the specific types passed to it, which is exactly what overloading provides.

questionText: What is 'subtype polymorphism' another name for?
option1: Static polymorphism
option2: Runtime polymorphism via inheritance/interface implementation (overriding)
option3: Operator overloading
option4: Method overloading
correctOptionExplanation: Subtype polymorphism refers to substituting a subtype object wherever a supertype is expected, achieved through overriding — i.e., runtime polymorphism.

questionText: Why can varargs methods sometimes create overload ambiguity?
option1: Varargs are never allowed to be overloaded
option2: Varargs disable polymorphism entirely
option3: Because a varargs method can match calls that could also match a fixed-arity overload, forcing the compiler to pick the more specific match
option4: Varargs always cause runtime errors
correctOptionExplanation: When both a fixed-parameter overload and a varargs overload could apply, the compiler prefers the fixed-arity match, but ambiguous cases can still cause compile errors.

questionText: How does autoboxing affect overload resolution?
option1: Autoboxing always causes a compile error in overloaded calls
option2: Autoboxing disables method overloading entirely
option3: The compiler prefers an exact-match overload (e.g., int) over one requiring autoboxing (e.g., Integer) when both are applicable
option4: Autoboxing is only relevant to overriding, not overloading
correctOptionExplanation: Java's overload resolution prioritizes matches without boxing/unboxing or varargs before considering those that require autoboxing.

questionText: What is the main risk of overusing method overloading with many similar signatures?
option1: It always breaks polymorphism
option2: Reduced readability and potential ambiguity about which overload actually executes for a given call
option3: It forces all methods to become abstract
option4: It prevents the class from compiling
correctOptionExplanation: Too many similar overloads can make it hard for readers (and sometimes the compiler) to reason about which method is actually invoked.

questionText: Which scenario below is true runtime polymorphism, not just overloading?
option1: Student.print() vs Student.print(String)
option2: A method with two overloaded versions with different parameter counts
option3: IDog ref = new Pomeranian(); ref.doBark(); calling the Pomeranian-specific bark implementation
option4: Declaring two constructors with different parameters
correctOptionExplanation: Calling an overridden method through a supertype/interface reference and getting the subtype's specific behavior is the hallmark of runtime polymorphism.

questionText: What is a 'functional interface' in the context of polymorphism and lambdas?
option1: An interface with exactly one abstract method, allowing lambda expressions to be used as its polymorphic implementation
option2: A class that implements multiple interfaces
option3: Any interface with multiple methods
option4: An interface that cannot be implemented
correctOptionExplanation: Functional interfaces (like IDog if it had one abstract method) can be implemented inline via lambda expressions, another flavor of polymorphism introduced in Java 8.

questionText: If IDog had exactly one abstract method, could you write `IDog d = () -> System.out.println("woof");`?
option1: No, lambdas require at least two abstract methods
option2: Yes, since IDog would qualify as a functional interface, letting a lambda serve as its implementation
option3: No, lambdas can only implement classes, not interfaces
option4: Yes, but only for abstract classes
correctOptionExplanation: A single-abstract-method interface can be implemented with a lambda expression, which the JVM treats as a polymorphic instance of that interface.

questionText: Why is polymorphism considered essential for writing testable code?
option1: It prevents subclasses from being created
option2: It makes all methods static, simplifying testing
option3: It removes the need for any test cases
option4: You can substitute a real implementation with a mock/fake object that shares the same interface during tests
correctOptionExplanation: Because test code can depend on the interface/abstraction, a mock implementation can be substituted at runtime without changing the code under test — a direct benefit of polymorphism.

questionText: In `trip.addExpense(hotel, hotelParticipants, null)` from the Splitwise example, if hotel is typed as Expense but is actually an EqualExpense object, what enables the correct split logic to run?
option1: The null argument determines which class executes
option2: Java picks the split logic randomly
option3: Overloading, since addExpense has multiple versions
option4: Runtime polymorphism — Expense's abstract split method dispatches to EqualExpense's implementation
correctOptionExplanation: Because EqualExpense overrides the abstract splitting behavior defined on Expense, calling it through the Expense reference still executes EqualExpense's specific logic at runtime.

questionText: Can you have both method overloading and method overriding involving the same method name in one class hierarchy?
option1: No, you must choose only one per hierarchy
option2: No, this always causes a compile error
option3: Yes, a subclass can overload additional versions of a method while also overriding the inherited one
option4: Yes, but only with static methods
correctOptionExplanation: A subclass can override the exact inherited signature and separately add new overloaded versions with different parameters — both can coexist.

questionText: What is the main difference between polymorphism and inheritance as concepts?
option1: Polymorphism requires no inheritance whatsoever in any language
option2: Inheritance is a runtime concept while polymorphism is compile-time only
option3: Inheritance establishes the IS-A relationship/mechanism; polymorphism is the resulting behavior of one call working differently across related types
option4: They are exactly the same concept with different names
correctOptionExplanation: Inheritance (or interface implementation) sets up the type relationship that makes polymorphism possible, but polymorphism specifically refers to the behavior of dispatching to the right implementation.

questionText: Why is polymorphism described as letting you 'write code once, use it for many types'?
option1: Because it eliminates the need to write any classes
option2: Because it converts all types into Object automatically
option3: Because it removes the need for interfaces
option4: Because logic written against a shared supertype or interface automatically works correctly for any current or future subtype
correctOptionExplanation: Code written against an abstraction handles any conforming implementation without modification, which is the core productivity benefit of polymorphism.
